title: Le scénario de Hartman  (Mathias and Isabelle)

segments.t: At a quiet restaurant in Paris, Mathias meets with superstar Isabelle Adjani to review an ambitious movie script. While Isabelle loves the dramatic depth of the project, Mathias cautiously warns her about the director's eccentric demands. Listen to the scene in French first.
C'est un scénario profond et intelligent.
C'est un art dramatique puissant.
C'est tout ce que j'aime.
C'est bien? Je vais conclure.
Vous devez savoir une chose importante.
Sacha Hartman n'est pas facile.
J'y suis habituée, tu sais.
Je peux être épuisante aussi.
Il fait chanter toute son équipe.
J'ai toujours adoré ta franchise.
S'il y a un problème, dis-le.
Hartman a choisi quelqu'un d'autre?
Andréa a été un peu vite.
Il pense à une actrice américaine.
Oui, bien sûr. C'est dommage.
Let's walk through the conversation step by step.
C'est un scénario profond et intelligent.
'It is a profound and intelligent screenplay.' Isabelle praises the artistic depth of the text. The paired adjectives follow the masculine singular noun.
C'est un art dramatique puissant.
'It is powerful dramatic art.' She expresses admiration for the intensity of the role. The descriptive adjective precedes the strong closing adjective.
C'est tout ce que j'aime.
'It is everything that I love.' The star connects passionately with the creative vision. The relative clause combines demonstrative pronoun with subject verb.
C'est bien? Je vais conclure.
'Is it good? I will close the deal.' Mathias prepares to negotiate contracts on her behalf. The near future tense announces immediate professional action.
Vous devez savoir une chose importante.
'You must know an important thing.' The agent issues a diplomatic preliminary warning. The semi-auxiliary verb precedes an infinitive of knowledge.
Sacha Hartman n'est pas facile.
'Sacha Hartman is not easy.' Mathias describes the director's notoriously stubborn temperament. The negative structure surrounds the third-person copula.
J'y suis habituée, tu sais.
'I am used to it, you know.' Isabelle brushes off the concern with experienced confidence. The adverbial pronoun stands in for difficult director relationships.
Je peux être épuisante aussi.
'I can be exhausting too.' The diva playfully acknowledges her own demanding reputation. The modal verb indicates personal capability followed by an adjective.
Il fait chanter toute son équipe.
'He makes his entire crew sing.' Mathias mentions an eccentric routine between rehearsal takes. The causative construction combines faire with an infinitive action.
J'ai toujours adoré ta franchise.
'I have always loved your frankness.' Isabelle values transparent communication from her agent. The compound past tense carries the adverb between auxiliary and participle.
S'il y a un problème, dis-le.
'If there is a problem, say so.' She invites direct truth about any casting obstacles. The imperative attaches the direct object pronoun with a hyphen.
Hartman a choisi quelqu'un d'autre?
'Did Hartman choose someone else?' Isabelle cuts straight to the central question. The indefinite expression refers to another prospective actor.
Andréa a été un peu vite.
'Andrea was a bit too hasty.' Mathias gently blames his colleague for premature promises. The adverbial modifier softens the assessment of haste.
Il pense à une actrice américaine.
'He is thinking of an American actress.' The agent reveals rival international interest. The prepositional verb introduces the competitor role.
Oui, bien sûr. C'est dommage.

'Yes, of course. It is a pity.' Isabelle acknowledges the setback with quiet dignity. The polite confirmation closes their candid mealtime discussion. Now listen to the whole scene again at normal speed, and see how much more you catch.

Oui, bien sûr. C'est dommage.
Although Mathias tries to shield Isabelle from disappointment, the star's curiosity is sparked by the elusive director. Listen to the French conversation one more time.
Je veux rencontrer ce réalisateur.
